{{Rhetoric}}

'''New rhetoric''' is an [[interdisciplinary field]]<ref name="Andreea">Andreea Deciu Ritivoi, ''Rhetorics: New Rhetorics'', in Wolfgang Donsbach (ed.), ''The International Encyclopedia of Communication'', {{doi|10.1002/9781405186407.wbiecr093}}</ref> approaching for the broadening of [[classical rhetorics|classical rhetorical canon]].<ref>Per example in ''Defining the New Rhetoric'' and ''Professing the New Rhetoric''</ref><ref name="DeGenaro">New and Alternative Rhetorics - William DeGenaro, ''Who says?: working-class rhetoric, class consciousness, and community'', Univ of Pittsburgh Press, 2007, p.5</ref>

==Overview==
"New" rhetoric is the name for various efforts to reclaim the study and teaching of [[rhetoric]] from the unsavory reputation<ref name="Andreea"/> it developed from association with "political lies, corporate spin ... [[purple prose]], [[Boilerplate text|boiler-plate]] arrangement schemas, unimaginative reproductions of bullshit and so on."<ref name="George">George Pullman, ''Rhetorically Speaking, What's New?'', Georgia State University, What is the New Rhetoric? conference</ref> The New Rhetoricians hoped to place rhetoric once again as a scholarly discipline <ref name="Andreea"/> at least to the level of other contemporary fields in social, cultural and linguistic studies. 

The field is often dated to [[Chaïm Perelman]]'s and [[Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca|Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca's]] ''The New Rhetoric'' (1969)<ref name="Thomas">Thomas M. Carr, Jr. ''Some Consequences of The New Rhetoric: A Critical Study'', Argumentation 7: 475-479, 1993</ref> but both the notion and the idea for the need of "new" rhetoric, different from the "old" one, can be traced to the works of [[Kenneth Burke]] - ''A Rhetoric of Motives'' (1950) and ''Rhetoric - Old and New'' (1967).<ref>Zachary M. White, [https://docs.lib.purdue.edu/dissertations/AAI3113888/ Re-examining Kenneth Burke on "identification" in the "new" rhetoric],  dissertation @ Purdue University</ref>

The emergence of New Rhetoric was helped by the idea that rhetoric could be [[epistemic]].<ref name="Andreea" /> An attempt to apply New Rhetoric as a social philosophy was made by the Polish philosopher [[Mieczysław Maneli]] in his 1994 book ''Perelman's New Rhetoric as Philosophy and Methodology for the Next Century''.<ref>Crosswhite, James ''Deep Rhetoric: Philosophy, Reason, Violence, Justice'', Wisdom, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2013 p.45-56</ref> Maneli wrote: "The New Rhetoric is modern [[humanism]]. The struggle for humanism never ends. The most essential features to a humanistic approach to life are: individuals should be given the chance to develop their personal talents and energies, they should be able to be creative and become happy...Their essence and value are creativity and self-determination...Once new rhetoric took as its basic proposition that nothing is absolutely good or sacred except human dignity, one must constantly search for new values, for better forms, and ways of life. There are three specific areas that is especially important for modern humanism: social and individual justice, freedom from oppression with a genuine opportunity for a decent life; and tolerance and privacy."<ref>Crosswhite, James ''Deep Rhetoric: Philosophy, Reason, Violence, Justice'', Wisdom, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2013 p.48-46</ref> 

New Rhetoric has an ambivalent relationship with Classical Rhetoric.<ref name="Andreea" /> For example, New Rhetoric attempts to break with the [[Formalism (philosophy)|formalistic]] and [[logocentric]] (i.e. [[patriarchal]]) [[Neo-Aristotelianism (literature)|Neo-Aristotelian]] analysis in favour of interplay between [[Text (literary theory)|text]] and [[Context (language use)|context]], but according to DeGenaro it does not successfully place itself outside the "Western-patriarchal" tradition, as it is unable to depart from "elite backgrounds and scopes of study"<ref name="DeGenaro" /> to a diversity of voices, topics, etc. This probably makes new rhetoric rather a ground for [[Postmodernism|postmodern]] rhetoric<ref>Not the rhetoric of [[postmodernism]] but postmodern theory and analysis in rhetorics.</ref> which "puts into question the identities of the speaker, the audience, and the messages that pass between them"<ref name="Gary1">Gary E. Aylesworth, ''Rhetoric, Postmodern'' ''The International Encyclopedia of Communication'', {{doi|10.1002/9781405186407.wbiecr069}}</ref> with evaluating the [[intersubjective]] philosophy<ref name="Barry">Barry Brummett, ''Some Implications of "Process" or "Intersubjectivity": Postmodern Rhetoric'', Philosophy & Rhetoric, Penn State University Press, 1976</ref> because of the idea inherently accepted in [[postmodern philosophy|postmodernistic philosophy]] that "differences cannot be overcome, in [[Hegel]]ian fashion, by cancelling them under a higher-order [[Sublation|synthesis]], but must be eroded or defaced in the course of traversing them".<ref name="Gary2">Gary Aylesworth, ''[http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/postmodernism/#8 Postmodernism]'', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy</ref>
